newsitem.title: USA: Species backlog keeps cat off U.S. endangered list.
newsitem.headline: Species backlog keeps cat off U.S. endangered list.

text.p: U.S. officials ruled Thursday that the Canada lynx was declining in number but they did not have the resources to protect the elusive cat under the Endangered Species Act.
An environmental group blasted the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's decision and charged that if the agency needed more money to protect endangered species, it should be asking the public for it.

The agency said while the Canada lynx's population had declined sharply in recent decades, there was already a backlog of mammals, reptiles and insects waiting for the protection of being listed as officially endangered species.

"We are currently precluded from proposing the Canada lynx for addition to the list until we are able to get to that backlog of other, higher-priority species," spokesman Michael Amaral told Maine Public Radio.
The small hunting cat has protected status in several states. Its range in the United States once included 22 states, but it can now be found only in Maine, Montana, Wyoming and Washington.

A federal judge had ordered the service to review a 1994 ruling that the lynx did not warrant listing, and the director of the environmental group Restore the North Woods called Thursday's ruling "ridiculous."

"How do we judge which wildlife deserves to survive and which doesn't?" Michael Kellet said. "If the agency needs more money and more resources ... then it should be asking for that and letting the public know."

The Canada lynx has a short black-tipped tail, long tufts on its ears and large, furry paws that allow it to hunt in deep snow. Males average about 22 pounds (10 km) in weight, while females are slightly smaller.
Loss of suitable forest habitat, hunting and inadequate efforts to protect the cat are among the reasons for its decline, according to wildlife officials.
Among the species the government considers to have higher priority for the endangered list are the boreal toad, the fat-world pond snail and the coral pink sand dunes tiger beetle.
